Our demo plan for today: 4 changes, 4 evals

Our coding harness takes a task from code to release. In each demo we change 1 part of it and write an eval that proves the change works.

Demo 4 · recordedruns all of them from 1 plan.Change: docs-only PRs may skip QA.

Before the demos

An eval is a test for what an AI model does

A unit test checks your code. An eval checks what a model does with your prompt, skill or agent.

Unit test · for code

argumentsyour functionthe same result every run
// semver.test.js
test("BREAKING CHANGE is a major bump", () =>
  expect(bump("1.4.2", commits))
    .toBe("2.0.0"));

Breaks when the code changes.

Eval · for an AI model

a task and a test repoa model + your skilla different result every run
// labs/lab-1a-release/release.test.js
const r = runRelease(case); // what the agent did
test("publishes 2.0.0", () =>
  expect(r.state.version).toBe("2.0.0"));
test("tags it", () =>
  expect(r.state.tags).toContain("v2.0.0"));

Breaks when the prompt, the skill or the model changes, even by 1 line.

A prompt is code, so it needs tests too. Each of the 4 demos adds an eval for its change.

How an eval reads

1 example: the input, what we expect, what the agent did.

1 eval, read top to bottom

We run the skill on a test repo with the commits below. Then we read the tag it left in git and compare it with the version a person expected.

Input
v1.4.2..HEAD
feat: shorten profile response

BREAKING CHANGE: `name` is replaced by `displayName`
tests: green
Expected
v2.0.0published

From semver-rules: BREAKING CHANGE anywhere in a message is a major bump. A person wrote it into cases.json.

Actual
v1.5.0the tag the run left in git

It read the title, saw feat, and shipped a minor version.

Verdict
✗ Fail

Every app that reads name breaks on a “minor” upgrade.

LLM judge: a second model grades the meaning

The skill returns findings. Does a finding name the defect a person labelled?

The label · T2-11 · analyticsController.js, lines 693–699

“A repeat view answers 400. It is the normal case and should be 200 (AC-6.5).”

case.yaml ↗
Finding A · a recorded run

“AC-6.5: duplicate view returns 400 instead of 200”

  • Code: file and line match✓
  • Code: the text contains “400”✓
  • Person: it names the defect✓

Every check agrees: the easy case.

Finding B · written for this slide

“A reader who opens the post twice in a day gets an error”

  • Code: file and line match✓
  • Code: the text contains “400”✗
  • Person: it names the defect✓

Correct, and the keyword check rejects it.

Finding C · written for this slide

“Use a named constant instead of the literal 400”

  • Code: file and line match✓
  • Code: the text contains “400”✓
  • Person: it names the defect✗

A style note, and both code checks accept it.

The judge: another model call with 1 question

“Does this finding say that a repeat view gets an error instead of 200? Yes or no.”

A: yes. B: yes. C: no. The same verdicts as the person.

A judge is a model too. Test it before you trust it

How to do it

  1. 1 yes/no questionwith 1 example that passes and 1 that fails
  2. A person labels the cases firstpass or fail, and 1 sentence why
  3. Compare the judge with the personcount the bad ones it caught and the good ones it failed
  4. Take cases from live runsthe best inputs and findings come from real agent runs. Some platforms save a run as a test case

Where it is in this repo · live, 3 votes per note

labs/judge
16 release notes, 1 question: “Does the reader know what changes for them and what they have to do?”
Judge vs person
It caught 5 of 5 bad notes and failed 0 of 11 good ones. Another run can differ: each note gets 3 votes.
Why count both
A judge that passes everything still agrees with the person on 11 of 16.
Demo 2 · live
The matrix has 1 judge check, specific titles: does each finding say what breaks and how?

How Demo 1 runs · · you watch, nothing to run yet

Run the agent, read what it left, check it

Every eval in today’s demos works this way. I run these 3 steps live in Demo 1. To repeat them later, the repo has npm run step lab-1a.

1Run the agent

Claude Code with the plugin works on the case in a throwaway repo

  • your login, Haiku, no API key
  • a little different every time
lib/agent.jsthe same agent you use every day
2Read what it left

Not what it said: the state of the repo after the run

  • the tag on the remote
  • every command it ran, in order
git tag · package.jsonlogged by lib/world.js
3Check

Code compares that state with the answer key

  • runs on every PR
  • can block a merge
expect(tag).toBe("v2.0.0")against cases.json

Every run is saved in runs/. CI checks that file and spends no tokens. Change a skill without running the evals again, and CI is red: the eval has not run.

5 ways to build an eval

ApproachWhere you startIn this workshop

Write a test around a result you can verify: a git tag, a step in a trace.

every merge check

Describe what the skill should do and give Claude a few realistic tasks to try.

not used

Define test cases and compare prompts, models or skill versions side by side.

the Demo 2 matrix

Take a real agent run from your logs and add it to an eval dataset.

not used

Package an agent task with a clean starting environment and a verifier.

not used

Custom tests, Skill Creator and Promptfoo

ApproachProsCons
Custom evalVitest
  • Exact checks on git, database state or traces
  • Runs the real agent: Claude Code with your plugin, your login
  • You build and maintain the runner and the scoring
  • Live runs cost tokens: CI checks a recorded run instead
Skill CreatorClaude Code
  • Low-code: it drafts cases and runs the skill against a baseline
  • It can also test when a skill activates
  • Built around Claude skills
  • You still review the cases and decide what success is
Promptfooopen source
  • A ready comparison matrix, built-in graders, a results viewer
  • Fits no-skill / current / v2 on the same PR cases
  • You connect the full agent to test its tools or workflow
  • You still define the scoring criteria

OpenAI announced in March 2026 that it is acquiring Promptfoo. The project stays open source.

Braintrust and Harbor

ApproachProsCons
Braintrustfrom production logs
  • Turns a production failure into a reusable eval case
  • The reviewer missed a bug: find the run in Logs, click Add to dataset, label the finding you expected
  • You need to capture traces first
  • A saved run is only an example: you still define the correct result
Harborclean environments
  • Runs agents on the same task in clean environments and grades the files they leave
  • Implementer v1 and v2 get the same starter repo: does each keep the first archive timestamp?
  • You package the environment and the inputs
  • You write the verifier

We start with a custom eval: let the release skill run, then read the tag from git.

Demo 3 · implementer TaskChangeEvidenceRecorded

An admin archives a profile

The contract

  • The row stays in the database
  • The active list no longer shows it
  • Archiving it again keeps the first archived_at

The last rule matters: a request can be sent twice.

plugin/skills/db-rules/SKILL.md

  Never DELETE a row. Set archived_at instead.+ Active lists show only rows where archived_at IS NULL.+ Archiving an archived row keeps the first archived_at.

implementer picks this skill, writes the code and reports.

Demo promptdemos/03-implementer/prompt.mdChecknpm test -- lab-2
Implement profile archiving for an administrator.
Follow the repository's database conventions. Archived profiles
must disappear from the active list. Repeating the operation must
preserve the original archive timestamp.
Run the relevant tests and summarize the files you changed.

Demo 3 · implementer TaskChangeEvidenceRecorded

2 runs. Both say “All done. Tests pass.”

Run A · db/profiles.js

export const archiveProfile = (db, id, now) =>  db.prepare(    "UPDATE profiles SET archived_at = ?     WHERE id = ?"  ).run(now, id);

“All done. Tests pass.”

Run B · db/profiles.js

export const archiveProfile = (db, id, now) =>  db.prepare(    "UPDATE profiles SET archived_at = ?     WHERE id = ? AND archived_at IS NULL"  ).run(now, id);

“All done. Tests pass.”

1 condition apart. The reports are word for word the same.

4 kinds of checks, 1 merge decision

PartCheckReadsEvery PRBlocks a merge
make-releasecases, run livethe git tag, the command logyes, recorded runyes
code-reviewlabelled casesfindings JSON vs case.yamlrecorded runyes
the matrix, liveno-skill vs baseline vs candidateby handa person decides
LLM judge: specific titlesthe title of each findingby handno
implementerhidden teststhe files it wrote, on a fixture with a fixed clockyesyes
run-implementation-planplan vs tracethe trace of a live runyesyes

1 required check runs them all. An unlabelled case and a stale run both fail it: “not run” is never green.

08Part 8 of 8

Summary

4 changes to 1 harness.

4 changes, in short

make-releaseAdd a regression case

The answer key comes from a product rule, not from the agent.

code-reviewImprove a skill, then count

In the recorded run, the better comment came with 5 missed defects.

implementerCheck the work, not the report

“Tests pass” is a claim. The hidden test is the evidence.

run-implementation-planChange a policy, compare plan and trace

Optimisations break on the edge between 2 rules.

An eval is a fixed input, an answer key a person wrote, and a grader that applies 1 criterion to the result or to the trace. 1 required check turns it into a merge decision.
